extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning discrete mathematics, combinatorics, and introductory proof techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for solving elementary counting problems (combinations, Pascal's triangle, inclusion–exclusion) and for writing clear direct proofs (definitions, case analysis, proof structure). Intended as textbook instruction and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binomial coefficient recursion (Equation 3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For integers n and k with 0 < k < n, C(n,k) = C(n-1,k) + C(n-1,k-1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combinatorial justification: count k-element subsets of an (n+1)-element set by splitting into those that contain a particular element (choose remaining k-1 from n) and those that do not (choose k from n). The identity expresses that total equals those two counts. Use this identity when constructing Pascal's triangle or computing coefficients without factorial formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pascal's Triangle construction rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange binomial coefficients in rows (Row n lists C(n,k) for 0 ≤ k ≤ n) with apex Row 0 = [1]; every interior entry equals the sum of the two entries immediately above it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: place 1 at each end of a row, compute each interior entry as sum of two numbers above. Rows correspond to coefficients of (x+y)^n. Use this method to compute rows (example: row 8 = 1 8 28 56 70 56 28 8 1) without applying the factorial formula directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binomial Theorem (Theorem 3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If n is a non-negative integer, (x + y)^n = Σ_{k=0}^n C(n,k) x^{n-k} y^k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: the coefficients in the expansion equal the entries in Row n of Pascal's triangle. Use this theorem to expand binomials and to extract specific coefficients in algebraic expressions (exercises demonstrate finding coefficients of monomials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Binomial Theorem for coefficient extraction
rubrics_metrics.description: To find the coefficient of a given term in (x+y)^n (or variants like (x+2)^n or (3x-2y)^n), apply the Binomial Theorem and read off coefficients using C(n,k) and the powers/factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical technique: look at Row n of Pascal's triangle or compute C(n,k) for relevant k; account for extra constants (e.g., 2^k or (-2)^k) when one term is scaled. Examples/exercises show multiple variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion–exclusion for two sets (Equation 3.3)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: counting |A| + |B| double-counts elements in A∩B, so subtract them once. Use to reduce a union-counting problem to counts of simpler sets (example: counting 3-card hands that are all red or all face cards). Recognize the anti-pattern of naively using |A|+|B| without checking intersection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion–exclusion for three sets (Equation 3.4)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use alternating inclusion and exclusion to correct overcounts when combining three sets. If pairwise intersections are empty, this reduces to simple sum; otherwise compute all necessary intersections. The text suggests understanding but postpones deeper combinatorics course for more complex cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition Principle (disjoint union rule, Fact 3.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A1, A2, ..., An are sets with Ai ∩ Aj = ∅ for i ≠ j, then |⋃_{i=1}^n Ai| = Σ_{i=1}^n |Ai|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condition of pairwise disjointness is essential. Use when partitioning a counting problem into mutually exclusive types — e.g., binary strings with 1,3,5,7 ones — and then sum counts for each type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count k-element subsets via combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of k-element subsets of an n-element set is C(n,k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this principle repeatedly in counting problems: selecting k items from n without order yields C(n,k). Applied directly in card-hand and binary-string examples; often the building block when applying inclusion–exclusion or partitioning cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partitioning into disjoint cases for counting
rubrics_metrics.description: When a set can be partitioned into disjoint subsets (types), count each type and sum their sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to count 7-digit binary strings with an odd number of 1's, partition by number of 1's (1,3,5,7) and apply the Addition Principle. Ensure the pieces are disjoint and cover all possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs must be understandable and convincing
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is a written verification that shows the theorem is definitely and unequivocally true; it should be understandable and convincing to anyone with the requisite background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure readers agree on exact meanings of terms and symbols used. A proof should avoid ambiguity and use clear logical steps, definitions, and accepted facts so that an appropriately prepared reader is convinced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions must be exact, unambiguous, and used properly
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition is an exact, unambiguous explanation of the meaning of a mathematical word or phrase; definitions are often written conditionally but interpreted biconditionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this book defined terms appear in boldface. Although authors commonly phrase definitions as 'If ... then ...', treat them as 'if and only if'. Use definitions to rewrite assumptions in proofs (e.g., 'x is odd' → 'x = 2a + 1 for some integer a').

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct proof outline (for 'If P then Q')
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove P ⇒ Q: begin by assuming P ('Suppose P.') and deduce Q ('Therefore Q.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus attention only on cases where P is true, since P ⇒ Q is automatically true when P is false. Between the first and last lines use logic, definitions, and standard facts to transform P into Q. The text recommends writing the first and last lines first and then filling the middle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use definitions and standard facts explicitly in direct proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply precise definitions (e.g., even, odd, divisibility) and accepted arithmetic/algebraic facts to move from hypothesis to conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate replacing 'x is odd' with 'x = 2a+1' and manipulating algebra to produce the desired form. Cite definitions (e.g., Definition 4.2, 4.4) in proofs and derive intermediate equations that match definition templates (e.g., showing x^2 = 2b+1 to prove oddness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reusing variable names in different contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: When introducing existential objects via definitions (e.g., 'there exists an integer c such that ...'), use fresh symbols to prevent confusion with existing variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text demonstrates using new letters (d,e instead of reusing c) when applying the definition of divisibility in nested contexts. This prevents symbol collision and preserves clarity of the logical chain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write proofs in stages and then clean up to paragraph form
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft proofs by sketching the top ('Suppose P') and bottom ('Therefore Q') and filling the middle, possibly jumping between ends; then rewrite as a coherent paragraph for presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early in learning, put each sentence on its own line for clarity; later write compact paragraph proofs. The process of sketching helps plan steps and avoid gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use case analysis when the statement's truth depends on distinct situations
rubrics_metrics.description: If the property or result differs depending on whether a parameter falls into mutually exclusive categories (e.g., n even vs odd), prove the statement separately for each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure cases are exhaustive (cover all possibilities). Examples: parity-based proofs and producing n for each multiple of 4. Show clear reasoning inside each case and combine to conclude the general claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating similar cases and 'Without loss of generality' (WLOG)
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple cases are essentially identical up to symmetry, it is acceptable to treat one case and indicate the others are analogous using 'Without loss of generality...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For transparency, beginners are encouraged to write out all cases; 'WLOG' may be used later but should be applied only when cases truly are symmetric. The text avoids abbreviating 'WLOG' and recommends explicit wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use previously proved propositions/theorems appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof may legitimately rely on earlier results (propositions, facts) to deduce new conclusions (e.g., monotonicity when taking square roots of positive numbers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite earlier propositions when needed and ensure the hypotheses of those results are satisfied before applying them. The example shows using a prior proposition to justify taking square roots and preserving inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic manipulation should produce the specific form required by definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: When the goal is to show an object satisfies a definition (e.g., an integer is odd/even or a divides b), manipulate expressions to reach the canonical form in that definition (e.g., 2b+1 or b = ax).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan backwards from the desired definition-form to identify intermediate algebraic steps; the text models working backward from the goal and then reversing steps to write the proof. Show explicit substitutions to identify the witness integer when existential form is needed.
